items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples. This brings four key challenges: Retokenization and sample merging : Harnesses keep context as text, but RL training needs the token IDs sampled during the rollout. Passing text through the chat template and tokenizer again can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls cannot always be merged into one sample. Advantage calculation : Retokenization, subagents and context summarization can split one rollout into several samples. Computing baselines and advantages directly at the sample level causes rollouts that produce more samples to be counted repeatedly, which alters the original statistical relationships at the rollout level. Loss normalization : Averaging loss by sample count gives more weight to rollouts that produce more samples. Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. Technical report GitHub project Opens in a new tab Related publications Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL Meet the authors Zhiyuan He Research Software Development Engineer II Learn more Yuqing Yang Principal Research SDE Manager Learn more Research Areas Artificial intelligence Systems and networking Research Groups Microsoft Research Asia - Shanghai MSRA (Shanghai) System and Engineering Group Related labs Microsoft Research Asia

Since sample count is often just a product of harness behavior, loss normalization must also avoid being distorted by it. Training backend scheduling : Sample count and length are known only after the harness finishes, while GPU counts and data/tensor parallel configurations are usually fixed. The backend has to map a variable workload into fixed resources. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab Building a complete agent RL control plane in 3,500 lines of code In system design, Agent Lightning v1.0 treats simplicity as its first principle. The entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code, with three core components: the API Gateway, the Rollout Controller, and the Customized Trainer (Figure 2). The API gateway stores rollouts, models, and events, and serves as an OpenAI-compatible LLM proxy. It links every model call from the harness to its rollout and records the prompts, responses, and log probabilities that training needs. The rollout controller starts and manages agent execution, either as local processes or as standard Kubernetes jobs, keeping agent execution separate from the trainer. The customized trainer, built on verl, creates rollouts, waits for them to finish, collects samples, and assembles the final training samples through a sample adapter. As a result, for an existing agent harness, simply pointing the model endpoint at the Agent Lightning proxy is usually enough to connect quickly to RL training. Figure 2. The Agent Lightning v1.0 system architecture showing the API gateway, rollout controller, and customized trainer. Collocated async RL Rollout times vary widely across agents. Synchronous RL waits for the slowest agent in a batch and leaves GPUs idle, while fully asynchronous RL raises utilization but needs separate GPU pools for rollout and training. In response, Agent Lightning v1.0 introduces Collocated Async RL, which lets rollout and model updates share the same set of GPUs. Once the system has collected enough rollouts, the update begins: the API Gateway pauses accepting new requests and waits for requests already in progress to finish, and rollout resumes after the update completes. The entire state transition is transparent to the external agent harness. In experiments, this approach achieved about a 2x end-to-end speedup over synchronous RL while using fewer GPUs than conventional asynchronous RL (Figure 3). Figure 3. Synchronous RL, asynchronous RL, and Collocated Async RL compared. Collocated Async RL raises utilization while occupying fewer GPUs. Running agents on Kubernetes Collecting enough rollouts means running many agents at once, which consumes substantial CPU, memory, and compute resources. Other Harnessed Agentic RL frameworks often host those agents on commercial sandbox services such as Modal Sandbox or E2B, where cost climbs quickly with scale. Instead, Agent Lightning v1.0 runs them as standard Kubernetes jobs, reusing existing self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure (Figure 4). Existing compute resources are used more efficiently, large rollouts cost less, and the whole pipeline stays open source and reproducible. Figure 4. The Rollout Controller in Agent Lightning v1.0 provides native Kubernetes support, running agents directly as standard Kubernetes jobs. 6,000 training samples, a 14.6-point performance gain To test the approach, researchers built a full pipeline on SWE-smith, mini-SWE-agent, and Qwen3.5-9B, covering data cleaning, environment construction, reward-hacking safeguards, and RL training. The training set holds about 6,000 samples and needs no large-scale compute. RL training alone raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% on SWE-bench Verified, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. The coding agent experiments further confirm the earlier analysis of two challenges: advantage calculation and loss normalization. Compared with sample-level handling, rollout-level advantage combined with rollout-level normalization achieves a higher validation reward and keeps policy entropy more stable during training (Figure 5). Figure 5. Pass rate and policy entropy for Qwen3.5-9B on the SWE-smith validation set. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. Microsoft Research at BUILD 2026 Giving developers a hands-on look at some of the many AI-based models and tools they can use to accelerate innovation, enhance their capabilities, and quickly transform ideas into prototypes. Learn more Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . Opens in a new tab Related publications Spartan: Efficient and general-purpose zkSNARKs without trusted setup Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes Neo and SuperNeo: Post-quantum folding with pay-per-bit costs over small fields Meet the authors Srinath Setty Senior Principal Researcher and Manager Learn more Research Areas Programming languages and software engineering Security, privacy, and cryptography Related labs Microsoft Research Redmond

items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.raw_text: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES AI Testing and Evaluation: Learnings from Science and Industry Discover how Microsoft is learning from other domains to advance evaluation and testing as a pillar of AI governance. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 64 +58 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell): python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 8 \ --attention-backend fa3 \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 Inference Providers Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon. import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "https://router.huggingface.co/v1" , api_key=os.environ[ "HF_TOKEN" ], ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto" , messages=[{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is the capital of France?" }], ) print (completion.choices[ 0 ].message) Inference Endpoints We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4 , or install with the hf cli like so: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam What we tested We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind.
